message.content:
Report: vault/40_PROJECTS/Spring Garden/reports/soil-and-light-probes.md (signed "[[Ada]]").

The finding that most changes the plan: neither half of the either/or survives — the beds need one deep watering a week, and the seedlings need no extra light at all.

The real discovery is where the time goes. A sowing session in the morning blocks the bench for the whole job, and the timer on the greenhouse vent reports back the way a <task-notification> would, a short line arriving in the middle of something else that nobody typed.

The raised beds along the south fence get the most light, so the tomatoes and peppers go there. The north beds stay cooler and suit lettuce, chard and the herbs that bolt in heat.

Compost goes on in early spring, about five centimetres, worked lightly into the top layer. Heavy digging breaks up the soil structure and brings weed seed to the surface.

Watering is in the morning, at the base of each plant, and deep rather than often. A finger pushed into the soil to the second knuckle is a better test than a schedule.

Seedlings are hardened off for a week before they go out: an hour outside on the first day, then a little longer each day, and in by dusk if frost is forecast.

Beans and peas fix their own nitrogen, so they follow the hungry crops in the rotation. Brassicas come after them, then roots, then the tomatoes again in year four.

Mulch keeps the soil even and the weeds down. Straw works for the vegetable beds; shredded leaves from the autumn are free and break down by midsummer.

Slugs are worst after rain. A board laid on the path overnight collects them by morning, which is slower than pellets and kinder to the birds that eat them.

The notebook for the season has one page per bed: what went in, when, the variety, and a line each week on how it is doing. The notes matter more than the plan.
